storyboard.claim: The most disturbing thing about the novel is not Humbert's acts themselves.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert sitting alone in a bare room — the cold open teases that the real horror is elsewhere.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Cold open.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets up a mystery: if not his acts, then what? The next beat answers.

storyboard.claim: His prose is so beautiful you forget to be horrified.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The manuscript in Humbert's hand — the writing IS the weapon.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers beat 0: the disturbing thing is the prose itself.
storyboard.addedInformation: The notes icon makes the prose physically visible as an object Humbert wields.

storyboard.claim: Nabokov built a meticulously constructed snare for the reader.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Nabokov gesturing at the funnel trap — the architect showing his design.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Zooms out from Humbert's prose to Nabokov's master plan.
storyboard.addedInformation: Separates author from narrator — Nabokov designed the trap, Humbert is the bait.

storyboard.claim: The bait of the trap is the breathtaking beauty of the English prose.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert holding the book — the beautiful text is the bait.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the trap's architect to its bait.
storyboard.addedInformation: The book in hand makes the text a tangible lure.

storyboard.claim: Pop culture has misunderstood Lolita for decades.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert standing in an ordinary street — the novel has been misread in the everyday world.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the text itself to how the world received it.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: no icon reads right for cultural misunderstanding; the callout carries it.

storyboard.claim: People wrongly call it forbidden romance or tragic love — the narrator rejects this.
storyboard.concreteVisual: No romance imagery — a heart icon would reinforce the wrong reading. The struck-through phrase does the rejection.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Specifies the misunderstanding: the romance label.
storyboard.addedInformation: The strike tells a muted viewer the phrase is being crossed out, not endorsed.

storyboard.claim: Based on close reading of the excerpts, the popular reading is a complete misread.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert examined under a magnifier — close reading reveals what casual reading missed.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: After striking forbidden romance, names it formally: a complete misread.
storyboard.addedInformation: The magnifier makes pouring over excerpts visible.

storyboard.claim: This is not a love story — it is literature's most elaborate crime scene, and the murder weapon is language.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert in the courtroom holding the book — the weapon is in his hand.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The thesis statement, replacing the crossed-out forbidden romance.
storyboard.addedInformation: The courtroom set frames it as a crime; the book in hand IS the weapon.

storyboard.claim: To understand the crime, we must examine Nabokov's setup closely.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Nabokov thinking — the architect contemplating his design.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the thesis to the method: how was the crime built?
storyboard.addedInformation: Nabokov on screen distinguishes the author's design from Humbert's performance.

storyboard.claim: The setting is late 1940s America, primarily 1947-48.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert arriving on an American highway — the time and place.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the analytical frame to the story world: where and when are we?
storyboard.addedInformation: The highway places us in mid-century America — motels, diners, the road.

storyboard.claim: We are never allowed to see this world objectively — only through Humbert's eyes.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The iceberg — we see only Humbert's curated surface, never the objective depths beneath.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The small-town world looks quaint, but we only see what Humbert shows us.
storyboard.addedInformation: The iceberg makes hidden reality below the surface visible without sound.

storyboard.claim: We are trapped entirely behind Humbert's eyes — he is an unreliable narrator.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The mask — Humbert's public persona is a false face over his true nature.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From never objectively to the reason: Humbert's mask controls what we see.
storyboard.addedInformation: The mask makes unreliable narrator visible — a false face is literally what he presents.

storyboard.claim: Humbert is a European emigre, a literature professor with impeccable diction.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert in a classroom holding a book — the professor with his credentials.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Character introduction: who is behind the mask.
storyboard.addedInformation: The classroom and book ground his identity as a professor — the education he will weaponize.

storyboard.claim: Behind the encyclopedic knowledge is a deeply monstrous secret fixation.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The shadow self — Humbert's dark inner nature lurking behind the scholar.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same scene, new information: beneath the professor is a predator.
storyboard.addedInformation: The shadow self icon makes the hidden predator visible alongside the respectable exterior.

storyboard.claim: He is NOT writing from a cozy academic study — that framing is rejected.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert sitting in a bare room — the struck-through phrase rejects the comfortable image.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Transition: where he writes matters, and it is not where you think.
storyboard.addedInformation: The strike tells a muted viewer the comfortable assumption is being crossed out.

storyboard.claim: He is writing from a prison cell, awaiting trial for murder.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Chains — Humbert is literally imprisoned. The icon reads as confinement.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers beat 14: not cozy — a prison cell.
storyboard.addedInformation: The chains make the imprisonment physical; the reveal lands the correction.

storyboard.claim: He addresses ladies and gentlemen of the jury — but the reader IS the jury.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert in court, pointing outward — the law icon frames the trial, his finger names the reader as juror.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From prison cell to courtroom: he is on trial, and we are judging.
storyboard.addedInformation: The pointing gesture breaks the fourth wall — you is the viewer.

storyboard.claim: His goal from the first syllable is to manufacture the reader's consent for his inexcusable acts.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The puppeteer — Humbert controlling the reader through rhetoric.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Now that we know we are the jury, this is his strategy: puppet us into agreement.
storyboard.addedInformation: The puppeteer icon makes the manipulation mechanism visible — he is pulling strings.

storyboard.claim: He does not try to deny the events — that would be too easy.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert talking openly in court — he confesses the acts, which makes his strategy more insidious.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Specifies the manipulation: not denial but reframing.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: no icon reads right for confessing while reframing; staging carries it.

storyboard.claim: He constructs an entire aesthetic architecture of prose to house his abuse.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert holding his manuscript — the writing is the architecture.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From he doesn't deny to what he does instead: builds a literary fortress.
storyboard.addedInformation: The notes make the prose tangible — the architecture is literally the manuscript.

storyboard.claim: He wants the reader to say I understand the artist's soul and excuse the inexcusable.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert on stage performing — he is giving a performance, not a confession.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The goal of the aesthetic architecture: audience forgiveness.
storyboard.addedInformation: The stage set frames his confession as theater — he is performing remorse.

storyboard.claim: He goes for the psychological jugular right on page one.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert with the book — the weapon aimed at the reader from the first page.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Transition to how the trap works in practice: page one.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the book in hand echoes beat 7, but the callout narrows to page one.

storyboard.claim: The opening incantation of the book is famous for a reason.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert sitting at his desk — about to write the famous opening.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Zooms into page one: the specific passage.
storyboard.addedInformation: The word incantation signals this is a spell, not just prose.

storyboard.claim: Humbert's opening: Lolita, light of my life, fire of my loins, my sin, my soul.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert speaking the words — no fire icon (not literal fire), no heart (not romance). The man reciting is the visual.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The incantation itself, first half.
storyboard.addedInformation: The words are Humbert's — hearing them from HIS mouth reframes them as manipulation, not poetry.

storyboard.claim: The phonetic passage: the tip of the tongue taking a trip of three steps down the palate.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert speaking — the words themselves are the subject.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the incantation — the second, phonetic half.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: pure recitation; the next beats will decode what the passage does.

storyboard.claim: It reads as pure poetry — the rhythm pulls you in, almost musical.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert speaking with calm confidence — the seduction is working.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The reader's first reaction to the incantation: it is beautiful.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: staging mirrors beats 23-24; the callout shifts from quoting to reacting.

storyboard.claim: More importantly, it is entirely manipulative — it controls you physically.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert pointing in abstract space — the analysis shifts from admiration to accusation.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Reversal: the pure poetry is actually a manipulation tool.
storyboard.addedInformation: The switch to abstract set signals we are now inside the analysis, not the story.

storyboard.claim: He forces your mouth, tongue, vocal cords to move exactly as he dictates.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert pointing outward — dictating, commanding the reader's physical response.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Specifies the manipulation: physical control through phonetics.
storyboard.addedInformation: The pointing gesture makes dictating visible — he is directing the reader.

storyboard.claim: Before you process the moral reality, he has cast a hypnotic spell over your body.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert reaching toward the viewer — casting the spell, drawing us in.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From physical control to its effect: hypnosis.
storyboard.addedInformation: The reaching gesture visualizes the spell being cast toward the audience.

storyboard.claim: He establishes absolute dominance over the narrative from the very first line.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert standing dominant in abstract space — he owns the narrative.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The result of the spell: total control.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: staging is minimal; the callout carries the idea after four analytical beats.

storyboard.claim: He is so arrogant — he openly knows he is playing the reader.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert with an arrogant smirk and the game icon — he treats this as a game he is winning.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From dominance to arrogance: he is enjoying the manipulation.
storyboard.addedInformation: The game icon makes playing us literal. The smirk is real arrogance, not fake happiness.

storyboard.claim: You can always count on a murderer for a fancy prose style — the ultimate confidence trick.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert speaking calmly — delivering the famous self-aware confession.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The specific quote that proves beat 30: he openly names himself a murderer.
storyboard.addedInformation: The narrator's exact words, corrected from ASR.

storyboard.claim: By admitting his unreliability, he paradoxically makes us trust him more.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert smiling — the con artist's charm. The wink that disarms us.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The paradox: confessing manipulation increases trust.
storyboard.addedInformation: The happy expression is the con: he smiles because the trick is working.

storyboard.claim: He disarms our skepticism by performing honesty about his dishonesty.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert standing calmly — skepticism disarmed, he has won this round.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The mechanism behind trust him more: our guard drops.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: staging is minimal after several abstract beats; the callout carries it.

storyboard.claim: He historicizes his predation by wrapping himself in the cloak of the great romantic poets.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Flow diagram: Cite the poets -> Claim destiny -> Predation excused.
storyboard.onScreenText: Flow: Cite the poets -> Claim destiny -> Predation excused
storyboard.relationToPrevious: New section: the specific defense mechanism using literary allusions.
storyboard.addedInformation: The diagram makes the strategy's logic visible as a chain the viewer can follow without sound.

storyboard.claim: He drops massive high literary allusions constantly — Virgil and others — as a shield.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The shield icon — literature is his armor. Humbert holds a book as defense.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Step 1 of the flow diagram enacted: citing the poets.
storyboard.addedInformation: The shield makes defensive use of literature visible — he hides behind great names.

storyboard.claim: He brings in the heavy hitters to justify his specific fixation.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert pointing toward shelves — invoking the great literary names.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Deepens the allusion strategy: not just any references, the biggest names.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the library setting and pointing gesture suggest citing authorities without an icon.

storyboard.claim: Humbert argues Dante fell in love with Beatrice when she was 9 years old.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert speaking — quoting Dante as precedent. No heart icon: the love is Humbert's spin, not real romance.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: First named example of the heavy hitters: Dante.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the historical figure Humbert weaponizes — the viewer sees who he hides behind.

storyboard.claim: Petrarch fell in love with his Laura, a 12-year-old — revealing the core of his manipulation.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert still speaking — second precedent. The repetition makes the pattern visible.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Second example parallels the first — the pattern is now clear.
storyboard.addedInformation: Two names in two beats makes the viewer see a strategy, not an anecdote.

storyboard.claim: Dante and Petrarch are untouchable pillars of Western literature — that is exactly why Humbert chose them.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert standing among books — sheltered by the untouchable names.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains WHY those two: their status makes them unassailable shields.
storyboard.addedInformation: Connects to the flow diagram at beat 34 — this is claim destiny in action.
